rationale: Studies of auditory cortex used sounds of all kinds; audible sound is the defining condition.
conditions: The listener can hear the audio (it is played at an audible level).

rationale: Level-dependence of auditory cortex responses was shown with controlled sound levels; the file's relative level change is only a proxy for level at the ear.
conditions: Playback volume is unknown; the change is relative to the recording.

rationale: Onset-responsive cortex was characterised with speech; abrupt onsets in media include non-speech sounds.
Oddball and sensory-change studies used unexpected deviants in simple sequences. Whether a sudden sound in media captures attention depends on expectation, attention and context.
conditions: The event is unexpected for the listener and not ignored.

rationale: Voice-area studies used speech and non-speech vocal sounds, which is what this feature detects.
Language-network studies used sentences the participants understood; transcribed words show that language is present, not that it is understood.
conditions: The listener understands the language being spoken.
The listener is attending to the speech.

rationale: Meaningful words engage semantic processing in listeners who understand them; naturalistic podcast stories (Huth et al. 2016) are a close match for spoken content.
conditions: The listener understands the language being spoken.

rationale: Naturalistic story studies show long-timescale integration in higher-order areas when a story is coherent and followed; lexical cues only suggest a story is being told.
conditions: The listener follows the story over time.
Interpretation depends on the listener's beliefs (Yeshurun et al. 2017).

rationale: Theory-of-mind studies asked participants to reason about beliefs and intentions; mental-state words are only a cue that such reasoning may be invited.
conditions: The listener engages with what speakers or characters think or want.

rationale: Music-selective components were identified with natural music clips; detected music is the same stimulus class.
Meta-analyses pooled studies where listeners experienced, or were expected to experience, pleasure or emotion. The music alone cannot establish that a listener does.
conditions: The listener finds this music pleasurable or emotionally moving.
Familiarity strongly changes responses (Pereira et al. 2011).

rationale: Shown to illustrate a genuine scientific disagreement about whether music structure is processed in language regions.
Song-selective responses were identified for sung music; this detection is low-confidence and may reflect speech over music.
Beat studies mostly used controlled rhythms; a naturalistic replication found rhythm-feature responses less reliable than timbral ones (Burunat et al. 2016).
conditions: The listener perceives the beat.

rationale: Any viewed image engages occipital visual cortex; movie studies confirm this for film.
conditions: The viewer is looking at the screen.

rationale: In natural movies, early visual areas tracked non-motion image changes such as illumination (single study).
conditions: The viewer is looking at the screen.

rationale: Motion-sensitive cortex responds to motion in natural movies; this app's motion estimate is a coarse proxy.
conditions: The viewer is looking at the screen.

rationale: Face-selective fusiform cortex responded to faces within an unconstrained feature film (Hasson et al. 2004) as well as to face photographs.
conditions: The viewer is looking at the screen.

rationale: Scene-selective regions respond to spatial layout in scene images; the feature is user-marked.
conditions: The viewer is looking at the screen.

rationale: Cuts often coincide with situation changes, but when those are controlled, cuts per se were not positively associated with perceived event boundaries (Magliano & Zacks 2011).
conditions: The cut marks a change of situation or action for the viewer.

rationale: Event-boundary studies used moments that observers judged to be transitions between events, which is what this user annotation marks.
conditions: Other viewers may place boundaries differently.

rationale: Humor studies time-locked responses to moments participants found humorous; a marked joke may not be understood or found funny by a given listener.
conditions: The listener understands the joke.

rationale: Appreciation responses were tied to moments participants enjoyed.
conditions: The listener finds it funny.

rationale: Two naturalistic film studies related suspense ratings (from other viewers) to frontal and parietal activity.
conditions: The viewer is invested in the story and experiences suspense.

rationale: Kept so that a marked surprise produces an explicit 'insufficient evidence' result.
Kept so that a marked emotional theme produces an explicit 'insufficient evidence' result.
Kept so that emotion words produce an explicit 'insufficient evidence' result.
